reference.source: Firestein & Kelley's Textbook of Rheumatology / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Classically presents with massive, painless, bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, often with fever, night sweats, and raised inflammatory markers
Extranodal disease occurs in a large proportion, involving skin, sinonasal tract, orbit, central nervous system, and bone
The defining histological feature is emperipolesis: intact lymphocytes and other cells engulfed within the cytoplasm of large histiocytes
The pathognomonic histiocytes are S100-positive and CD1a-negative, distinguishing them from Langerhans cells
Most cases are sporadic and self-limiting, but disseminated or vital-organ disease can be aggressive
It may coexist with autoimmune or lymphoproliferative disorders and with other histiocytoses
Treatment ranges from observation for limited disease to corticosteroids, surgery, or systemic therapy for extensive or organ-threatening involvement
reference.pathophysiology: Rosai-Dorfman disease is a histiocytic proliferative disorder characterised by accumulation of large, activated histiocytes derived from the monocyte-macrophage lineage within lymph node sinuses and extranodal tissues. The hallmark is emperipolesis, the presence of intact inflammatory cells within histiocyte cytoplasm. Although historically considered reactive and possibly infection- or immune-triggered, a subset harbours clonal MAPK pathway mutations, placing it within the histiocytic neoplasm spectrum. The infiltrating S100-positive histiocytes expand lymph nodes and infiltrate extranodal sites, producing the clinical manifestations.
additionalInvestigations: Excisional lymph node or tissue biopsy demonstrating emperipolesis within S100-positive, CD1a-negative histiocytes
Full blood count and inflammatory markers (often raised ESR and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinaemia)
Cross-sectional imaging (CT/MRI) to map nodal and extranodal disease
MRI of brain and orbit when central nervous system or orbital involvement is suspected
Molecular testing for MAPK pathway mutations in atypical or aggressive cases
Screening for associated autoimmune or lymphoproliferative disorders
redFlags: Central nervous system or spinal involvement causing neurological deficit
Airway or orbital compromise from bulky masses
Vital-organ infiltration (kidney, liver, lower respiratory tract) associated with worse outcomes
Features suggesting concurrent lymphoma or autoimmune disease
reference.prognosis: Most patients, particularly those with isolated nodal disease, follow a benign self-limiting or relapsing-remitting course, but extensive extranodal disease, central nervous system involvement, or associated immune dysregulation confers a more guarded prognosis.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting the histiocytic infiltrate as lymphoma and missing emperipolesis
Failing to use S100 and CD1a staining to distinguish it from Langerhans cell histiocytosis
Overtreating limited disease that would resolve spontaneously
Underestimating the extent of extranodal or central nervous system involvement
Not looking for associated autoimmune or lymphoproliferative conditions
management: Observation for asymptomatic isolated nodal disease, given the frequent spontaneous regression
Surgical excision or debulking of symptomatic, localised or compressive lesions
Corticosteroids as first-line systemic therapy for symptomatic or extranodal disease
Systemic chemoimmunotherapy such as vinblastine, methotrexate or mercaptopurine for refractory or disseminated disease
Targeted MAPK-pathway inhibition with MEK or BRAF inhibitors where clonal kinase mutations are identified
Radiotherapy for critical-site disease threatening vital structures such as the central nervous system or orbit when otherwise uncontrolled
Screening for and management of coexisting autoimmune or lymphoproliferative disorders, with multidisciplinary haematology and immunology input
